title: Ezra 6:13–22
context: Ezra 6:13–22 records the completion and dedication of the temple and the Passover that follows. Tattenai carries out Darius’s decree, and the elders build and prosper through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah, finishing the house according to the commandment of the God of Israel and the decree of the Persian kings. It is completed on the third of Adar in the sixth year of Darius, commonly dated to about 516–515 BC. The returned exiles dedicate it with joy, offering sacrifices and twelve male goats as a sin offering for all Israel, and they arrange the priests and Levites as written in the book of Moses. The Aramaic section ends at 6:18, and the account of the Passover is in Hebrew. The priests and Levites purify themselves, and the returned exiles, joined by those who had separated themselves from the impurity of the nations to seek the LORD, keep Passover and the feast of unleavened bread with joy, because the LORD had turned the heart of the king toward them. The completion according to God’s commandment is shared ground for both traditions, which read the passage as God fulfilling his promise to restore his people’s worship.

verses.text: Then Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, Shetharbozenai, and their companions did accordingly with all diligence, because Darius the king had sent a decree.
verses.arminianNotes: Tattenai, Shetharbozenai, and their companions do as Darius commanded, with all diligence. Arminians see the officials obeying the king, which shows that the threat to the work has been removed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s providence fully at work. Both traditions read the verse as showing the officials’ cooperation, without suggesting they had been enemies of the work beyond what the text says.

verses.text: The elders of the Jews built and prospered, through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. They built and finished it, according to the commandment of the God of Israel, and according to the decree of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes king of Persia.
verses.arminianNotes: The elders build and prosper through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah, finishing according to the command of the God of Israel and the decree of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes. Arminian readers see God’s word and human obedience working together to finish the house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the work was completed according to God’s command, which is shared ground. Both traditions note that Artaxerxes reigned later (Ezra 7), and they read his name as part of a summary of Persian support.

verses.text: This house was finished on the third day of the month Adar, which was in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king.
verses.arminianNotes: The house is finished on the third of Adar in the sixth year of Darius. Arminians see faithful work brought to completion after many years of delay and opposition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God fulfilling his promise to restore his house. Both traditions note that the date is commonly placed around 516–515 BC, and they hold the precise chronology with appropriate caution.

verses.text: The children of Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the rest of the children of the captivity, kept the dedication of this house of God with joy.
verses.arminianNotes: The children of Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the returned exiles dedicate the house with joy. Arminian readers see joy as the fitting response to God’s faithfulness after the long years of exile and delay.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the whole community rejoicing in God’s work. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about joy in worship, and they compare the dedication of Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 8; 2 Chronicles 7).

verses.text: They offered at the dedication of this house of God one hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs; and for a sin offering for all Israel, twelve male goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: They offer a hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and twelve male goats as a sin offering for all Israel, one for each tribe. Arminians see the returned community identifying itself with all twelve tribes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the twelve goats expressing the unity of God’s people. Both traditions note that the offerings are much smaller than at Solomon’s dedication (2 Chronicles 7:5), yet they read the worship as fully accepted by God.

verses.text: They set the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their courses, for the service of God which is at Jerusalem, as it is written in the book of Moses.
verses.arminianNotes: They set the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their courses for the service of God, as written in the book of Moses. Arminian readers see worship ordered according to God’s word, which marks the returned community’s commitment to obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress the authority of the written law of Moses. Both traditions note that the Aramaic section of Ezra ends with this verse, and they read it as shared ground about worship shaped by Scripture.

verses.text: The children of the captivity kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month.
verses.arminianNotes: The returned exiles keep the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. Arminians see the community remembering God’s great act of deliverance from Egypt, now celebrated after a second deliverance from exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the date follows the command in Exodus 12:6. Both traditions read the Passover as shared ground about God’s faithfulness in redeeming his people.

verses.text: Because the priests and the Levites had purified themselves together, all of them were pure. They killed the Passover for all the children of the captivity, for their brothers the priests, and for themselves.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests and Levites have purified themselves, and they kill the Passover for all the returned exiles, their fellow priests, and themselves. Arminian readers see careful preparation for worship, showing reverence for God’s holiness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the purification as obedience to God’s requirements. Both traditions read the verse as showing the priests and Levites serving the whole community in the Passover.

verses.text: The children of Israel who had returned out of the captivity, and all who had separated themselves to them from the filthiness of the nations of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel, ate,
verses.arminianNotes: The returned exiles eat, together with all who had separated themselves from the impurity of the nations of the land to seek the LORD. Arminians see the community open to those who turn to God, joining the people of Israel in faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God drawing others to himself. Both traditions note that the identity of those who joined is not fully explained, and they read the verse as showing that seeking the LORD, not ancestry alone, marked the gathered worshipers.

verses.text: and kept the feast of unleavened bread seven days with joy; because the LORD had made them joyful, and had turned the heart of the king of Assyria to them, to strengthen their hands in the work of God, the God of Israel’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: They keep the feast of unleavened bread seven days with joy, because the LORD made them joyful and turned the heart of the king of Assyria to strengthen them in the work. Arminian readers see joy as God’s gift and his hand in the king’s favor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress God’s sovereignty over the king’s heart (compare Proverbs 21:1). Both traditions note that the title king of Assyria refers here to the Persian king, and interpreters offer different explanations for it.
